title: Who is speaking in Manu's book
hook: the Manusmriti opens with sages asking Manu, and Bhrigu speaking
carry: smriti is remembered, so ask who remembered it
tomorrow: does the law book ever bend its own rules? and for whom?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Manusmriti: a smriti set beside the Veda, with hard verses, and its own list of where dharma comes from, with conscience last. Today, a look back over the week, and who is actually speaking in that book.
screen: `READ IT WHOLE. SAY WHAT IT SAYS.`

segments.voice: The assignment lands on a Friday: senior seminar, pick one text and read it critically. Some kids pick a novel, some a famous speech. Priya stares at the list for a long time, then types in the book that guy in her comments keeps quoting: the Manusmriti. Her dad, Arjun, reads over her shoulder and says, dryly: bold. Then he adds: you know who's actually talking in that book, right?
screen: `PICK ONE TEXT. READ IT CRITICALLY.` → `'BOLD.'` → `WHO'S ACTUALLY TALKING?`

segments.voice: Here's the answer, and it's one to pass on. The Manusmriti opens like a scene. Great sages come to Manu as he sits with a collected mind, honor him, and ask him to teach them the duties of every class of people. Manu agrees and starts at the very beginning, with the making of the world. Then, still in the first chapter, he tells how the teaching reached him: the Creator taught it to him first, and he taught it to Marichi and the other first sages. And now, he says, Bhrigu here has learned the whole of it from me, and he will tell it to you. Bhrigu, pleased, begins. So the book presents itself as a teaching handed down, teacher to student. That frame carries a big Hindu idea in its very name. The Veda is shruti, what was heard, held to be revealed to the ancient seers. A book like Manu's is smriti, what is remembered, handed down by people, one to the next. That's why Hindu teachers have long weighed smriti against the Veda and against each other, and why a critical reader asks who did the remembering, for whom, and who wasn't in the room. Now the week, in one breath. The Buddha, honored as Vishnu's form, his story still Buddhist. Descents beyond counting. Kalki, still to come. The Kali age, with one door: sing the name. A wheel of ages turning back to truth. And dharma with four sources, not one book.
screen: `SAGES ASK MANU FOR THE DHARMA.` · `MANU HANDS IT TO BHRIGU.` · `SHRUTI: HEARD. SMRITI: REMEMBERED.` · `THE WEEK, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `ASK WHO REMEMBERED IT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and think of the first prayer, mantra or story about right and wrong you were ever taught. Who taught it to you? And who taught them? That chain, teacher to student, is how smriti travels; Hindus call it parampara. If you weren't raised with prayers, pick any first lesson about what's right. Just notice the faces in the chain, and notice too whose face is missing. Breathe with them for the rest of the sit.
The Manusmriti: the laws of Manu, a smriti, what is remembered, which the book frames as Bhrigu passing on Manu's teaching to the sages.
Carry this: smriti is remembered, so ask who remembered it, and who wasn't in the room. That's the week.

fork.setup: a classmate says: Hindus count the Buddha as Vishnu, so Buddhists are basically Hindus. what's the fair reply?
options: some Hindu texts tell him that way; Buddhists tell him as their own teacher.
right: the Bhagavata settles it, so the two are one religion.
wrong: no Hindu text ever mentions the Buddha at all.
fork.reveal: say whose telling it is: the Bhagavata and Jayadeva place him in Vishnu's line; Buddhists tell him as their teacher, and it's theirs to tell.

original.note: Sanskrit: Bhrigu, the sage who, in the book's own frame, retells Manu's teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: Manu sat down and wrote it all himself, and it counts the same as the Veda.
what it means: it's smriti, what is remembered: sages ask Manu, and Manu hands the telling to his student Bhrigu.
what a scholar hears: Manu 1.1–4 and 1.58–60, a framed text; 2.10, shruti is the Veda and smriti the dharma texts; so critical readers ask who speaks, and who isn't in the room.
recall: two tellings: say whose it is

chat.meaning: The book frames itself as smriti, teaching handed down: sages ask Manu for the dharma, and Bhrigu tells it. Reading critically starts with who remembered it, for whom, and who's missing.

tie.story: Sages asked Manu for the dharma, and Manu handed the telling to his student Bhrigu, who speaks the book.
tie.friend: Priya can start her paper by asking who remembered and passed on this smriti, and whose voices aren't in it.
tie.you: whose voice is missing from a rule you live by?

Bhrigu.meaning: Manu's student, who retells the teaching in the book

Manu.meaning: the ancestor-sage to whom the book is credited

Manusmriti.meaning: the laws of Manu, an old dharma text in verse

dharma.meaning: what is right; duty; the order that holds life together

shruti.meaning: what was heard: the Veda, held to be revealed to the seers

smriti.meaning: what is remembered: tradition handed down, like Manu's book

parampara.meaning: the chain of teachers, each passing the teaching to the next

sources.ref: Manusmriti 1.1–4 (the great sages approach Manu and ask for the dharma)
Manusmriti 1.58–60 (Manu says Bhrigu learned the whole from him and will teach it; Bhrigu speaks)
Manusmriti 2.10 (shruti is the Veda; smriti the dharma texts)

notes: Week end (1562–1568), review shape: the teach looks back over the week (Buddha 1562–1563, Kalki 1564–1566, Manusmriti 1567) and teaches the day's word lightly through the book's frame. Recall holds six recent words.

Paraphrase of Manu 1.1–4 (the great sages approach Manu) and 1.58–60 (Manu says Bhrigu learned the whole from him and will recite it; Bhrigu then speaks). 'As the book frames itself' is deliberate: the frame is the text's own, not a claim about who composed it. Confirm verse numbers.
